newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec plans '98 income tax cut and sales tax hike.
newsitem.headline: Quebec plans '98 income tax cut and sales tax hike.

text.p: Quebec Finance Minister Bernard Landry introduced a budget on Tuesday that proposed a personal income tax cut and an offsetting provincial sales tax hike next January.
In his speech to the provincial legislature, Landry also forecast as expected a C$2.2 billion deficit in 1997/98. Landry said Quebec was on track to balance its budget by fiscal 1999/2000.
"With the budget I am tabling today, we remain on course and will thus achieve a crucial step on the road to a zero deficit," Landry said.

The French-speaking province's budget deficit was C$3.2 billion in the year ending March 31, and was forecast to decline to C$2.2 billion in the new fiscal year and C$1.2 billion in 1998/99, Landry said.

To meet its 1997/98 deficit target, Quebec is cutting its program spending by C$304 million to reach C$34.4 billion. Revenues are forecast at C$38.1 billion, while debt service costs are forecast at C$5.9 billion in 1997/98.
In his budget, Landry also proposed a "major reform" of the province's taxation system beginning on January 1, 1998 which he expected to be revenue neutral for the government.
A reduction in personal income tax of C$850 million will be offset by an increase in the Quebec sales tax to 7.5 percent from 6.5 percent on January 1.

Under the reform, households whose total family income is less than C$50,000 a year, which account for 77 percent of Quebec households, will see their income tax reduced by 15 percent, for a total decrease of C$588 million.
Income tax payable by households earning more than C$50,000 annually will decrease by about three percent, for a total decrease of C$253 million.
Analysts said the income tax cut and sales tax increase were a surprise, but were credible measures since other Canadian provinces had moved toward reducing income tax levels.
"In 1998, Landry is putting on a net basis C$500 million more into the pockets of Quebec households," accountant Michael Tinkler told Reuters.
Landry said the tax reform was needed because Quebec's personal income tax burden was the highest of all G7 countries, of which Canada is a member.
Economists said Landry appeared to have a good chance of meeting his deficit target for 1997/98, mainly because Quebec's economy was showing signs of stronger growth.
"I believe they are on track and I believe their economic assumptions are conservative," Lise Bastarache, senior economist at Royal Bank of Canada, said.

Bastarache said she expected Quebec's economy to grow by 2 to 2.5 percent in 1997, compared with about 3 percent for all of Canada. In his budget, Landry forecast growth in Quebec's real gross domestic product of 1.5 percent in 1997 and 2.5 percent in 1998.
Bastarache said Quebec's economy should grow in a more balanced fashion this year, with consumer spending contributing to already robust advances in exports.

Landry said employment growth was a priority for Quebec, whose unemployment rate he forecast to hover near 11.5 percent for the next three years. Landry announced a plan to contribute C$250 million toward the creation of a private sector fund that would finance C$2.2 billion of projects.
Landry expects 25,000 new jobs in Quebec this year.
He said his budget was designed to boost Quebec's credibility and prepare it for the future.
"Our drive toward economic and financial health ties in perfectly with our progress toward our national destiny," Landry said.
Analysts expect the separatist Parti Quebecois government to call a provincial election in 1998 or 1999, and to hold another referendum on Quebec separation if it wins the vote.
